Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the MediCore Devices Second Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone. Please note, this call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements, including expectations regarding our future performance, business outlook, and financial results. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Joining me on today's call are Alex Rivera, CEO; Jordan Lee, CFO; Dr. Emily Chen, Chief Technology Officer; and Michael Torres, Chief Commercial Officer.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. MediCore Devices had a productive second quarter, marked by significant advancements in our product portfolio and expansion into new markets.

Today, I will cover six key aspects of our performance:
1. Procedure volume trends and market recovery commentary
2. Competitive dynamics and market share trends
3. Capital equipment vs consumables mix trends
4. Revenue and margin guidance for the next quarter/year
5. Key assumptions underlying the guidance
6. Gross margin trends and supply chain commentary

Jordan will then provide a more detailed review of our financials. Emily will follow with updates on our R&D initiatives, and then we'll open the call for your questions.

Now, let's get started with procedure volume trends and market recovery commentary.

As we discussed in our prepared remarks, we delivered another quarter of strong top-line growth, with global revenues up 14% as reported, or 12% organically. A key driver of this performance continues to be the robust recovery in procedure volumes across our core franchises, which marked the strongest quarter yet in our post-pandemic rebound. Let me dive into the details segment by segment and region by region, before sharing some strategic insights and our outlook.

Starting with the big picture: Global procedure volumes grew 16% year-over-year in Q2, accelerating from the 12% growth we saw in Q1. This brings us to 98% of pre-COVID levels on a two-year stacked basis, with elective procedures now fully normalized in most markets. Pent-up demand from 2020-2021 deferrals has largely played out, but we're seeing sustained momentum from secular tailwinds like an aging demographic—global over-65 population projected to grow 3% annually through 2030—shifting reimbursement dynamics favoring outpatient settings, and the ongoing migration to minimally invasive therapies. Our backlog of confirmed procedures stood at $2.8 billion at quarter-end, up 11% sequentially, signaling strong visibility into the second half.

Breaking it down by franchise, let's start with our Structural Heart segment, which remains our highest-growth area. Procedure volumes here surged 22% YoY, driven by transcatheter aortic valve replacement—or TAVR—growth of 28%, outpacing the broader market as tracked by our Milliman procedure data. Our next-gen EvoFlow TAVR valve, launched in the U.S. and EU earlier this year, captured 15% share in first-line implants within 90 days of approval, thanks to its 20% reduction in paravalvular leak rates versus predicate devices like Edwards' Sapien 3 Ultra. We also saw mitral clip volumes up 18%, bolstered by our partnership with an undisclosed academic center for a pivotal trial on functional MR, which is enrolling ahead of plan at 250 patients per month. Average selling prices, or ASPs, held firm at +2% YoY, offsetting any mix shift toward higher-acuity cases.

In Electrophysiology and CRM—cardiac rhythm management—volumes expanded 14% YoY, with ablation procedures up 19% on the back of our PulseField pulsed-field ablation platform, now live in over 200 U.S. centers. This technology addresses the safety concerns around thermal ablation, like esophageal injury, and has driven a 25% increase in de novo AFib cases. Pacemaker and ICD implants grew more modestly at 9%, reflecting some normalization post-COVID surge, but our leadless Micra AV device hit a record 45% of our U.S. CRM volume, up from 32% a year ago.

Orthopedics and Spine showed more measured recovery, with volumes up 8% YoY—hips and knees at +10%, spines flat. This franchise is still grappling with surgeon staffing shortages and cement supply constraints reminiscent of the 2021 DePuy Synthes recall issues, but we're gaining traction with our Trinity Cementless Acetabular System, which features a 30% faster surgical time via robotic optimization compatible with Stryker's Mako platform. U.S. knee ASPs rose 4% on premium mix, though international pricing pressures capped overall growth.

Endoscopy and Urology rounded out at 13% volume growth, led by 17% in robotic-assisted procedures using our FlexiScope single-use endoscope, which reduces cross-contamination risks by 95% compared to reusables—a big win amid ongoing infection control scrutiny post-Clostridium difficile outbreaks. Stone management with our VaporLase holmium laser grew 12%, capturing share from Boston Scientific's Competitor line.

Regionally, the U.S. led with 15% procedure growth, now at 102% of pre-COVID volumes. CMS reimbursement hikes for TAVR under the 2023 OPPS final rule—up 5.2% for hospital outpatient—combined with our 300+ hospital value analysis committee wins, fueled this. Medicare Advantage penetration at 48% of procedures is a tailwind, as plans prioritize high-acuity, site-neutral care.

EMEA grew 11% YoY, reaching 95% recovery, with Germany and the UK leading at +14% thanks to DRG adjustments and NICE endorsements for our TAVR portfolio. France lagged at +7% due to tariff negotiations, but our Paris-based manufacturing ramp mitigated FX headwinds from the weakening euro.

Asia-Pacific was the star at 21% growth, with China up 25% on the heels of NMPA approval for three new SKUs, including our TAVR valve. Procedure volumes there hit 110% of pre-COVID, driven by the "Healthy China 2030" initiative expanding structural heart access in Tier 2 cities. Japan grew 16%, benefiting from our J-MITRA clip IDE enrollment, while India accelerated 30% via partnerships with Apollo Hospitals for 50 new endoscopy suites.

Latin America trailed at 9% growth, still at 88% recovery amid Brazil's currency volatility and delayed elective restarts, but our Mexico City hub is positioning us for 15% H2 acceleration.

On the technical front, we're investing heavily in enabling technologies to sustain this momentum. Our AI-driven Procedure Optimization Platform, integrated across franchises, uses real-time imaging analytics to boost first-pass success rates by 18%—early data from 5,000 TAVR cases shows a 12% reduction in LOS, directly supporting our outpatient shift strategy. We've also deployed $150 million in supply chain resilience, including dual-sourcing nitinol for stents and expanding sterile packaging in Singapore, which de-risked Q2 volumes from the Red Sea disruptions.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on three pillars: (1) Portfolio pruning—divesting our legacy mechanical heart valve line for $200 million to fund high-growth TAMs like LAA occlusion, where we're targeting 20% share by 2025 via our next-gen Watchman FLX competitor; (2) M&A firepower with $1.2 billion dry powder for tuck-ins in neuromodulation, eyeing assets like Nevro's HF10 tech amid their recent distress; and (3) Commercial excellence, with our Surgical Intelligence suite now in 40% of U.S. ORs, delivering 5-7% utilization uplift through predictive scheduling.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 procedure volumes to grow 14-16% YoY, with H2 accelerating to 17% on seasonal tailwinds and new launches like our renal denervation system for hypertension—a $5 billion TAM underserved since the Paradise trial setback. Risks remain around hospital labor—nurse vacancy rates at 18% per AHA data—and potential U.S. recessionary pullback in electives, but our 65% recurring revenue mix from service and disposables provides insulation.

We're excited about the durability of this recovery—it's not just a snapback; it's underpinned by innovation and demographics.

Now, let's talk about competitive dynamics and market share trends.

I'll now turn to our competitive landscape and market share trends, which continue to validate our leadership position in the structural heart and minimally invasive robotics segments of the medical devices market. As you know, the global medical devices industry is navigating a dynamic environment shaped by post-pandemic procedure backlogs, accelerating adoption of robotic-assisted surgery, and intensifying competition from both incumbents and disruptors. According to recent IQVIA data, the overall market grew 6.2% year-over-year in Q2, reaching approximately $540 billion annualized, with structural heart devices expanding at a robust 9.8% CAGR through 2028, driven by transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) volumes and left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) procedures.

Let me start with the headline: we gained 180 basis points of global market share in structural heart over the past 12 months, bringing our total to 24.7%, up from 22.9% a year ago. This marks our third consecutive quarter of share expansion, outpacing the segment average. In robotics, where we're the #2 player behind Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci platform, we captured 1.2 points to reach 18.4% share in hybrid robotic systems for cardiac and neuro interventions—our VersaBot Xi platform now powers over 12% of U.S. TAVR procedures, per DARPM analytics.

Competitively, Medtronic remains the gorilla in the room with their CoreValve Evolut platform holding steady at 32% structural heart share, bolstered by their recent U.S. FDA approval for a next-gen low-profile valve that shaved 15% off deployment times. They've been aggressive on pricing, with ASPs down 4-6% in Europe amid tender pressures, but their share dipped 50 bps sequentially due to supply chain hiccups in their Chinese manufacturing. Boston Scientific, our closest rival in LAAO with their Watchman FLX at 28% share, saw flat performance as procedure growth slowed to 7% YoY—below our 11%—partly from reimbursement headwinds in Medicare Advantage plans. Meanwhile, Edwards Lifesciences, the TAVR kingpin at 41% share, reported softer-than-expected 8% procedure growth, ceding 90 bps to us on the strength of our AetherEdge valve's superior 95% one-year durability data from the pivotal ORBIT-3 trial.

On the robotics front, Intuitive's installed base grew 14% to over 8,700 systems globally, but their single-use instrument ASPs rose 3% to $2,800 per procedure, pricing some community hospitals out. This created an opening for our VersaBot, which offers modular reusables at 25% lower cost-per-case—$1,950—and we've seen 22% attach rate growth on our AI-driven navigation software, now with 98% accuracy in real-time tissue mapping. Smaller players like Auris Health (Johnson & Johnson) and Vicarious Surgical are nipping at heels with Monarch and single-port systems, but they're sub-5% share and focused on niche bronchoscopy, leaving the cardiac robotics arena to us and Intuitive.

Regionally, our trends are bifurcated but positive. In the U.S., which accounts for 42% of our revenue, we expanded share by 220 bps to 27.1% in structural heart, fueled by 15% TAVR volume growth amid CMS reimbursement parity for next-gen valves at $28,500 ASP. Europe, 28% of sales, saw us gain 140 bps to 21.8%, despite Germany's DiGA pricing reforms compressing margins by 2 points—our CE Mark for VersaBot's neuro module opened doors in the UK and France, where robotic procedures surged 19%. China, now 12% of total (up from 9% last year), is a bright spot: we hit 11.5% share via our JV with Mindray, navigating NMPA approvals faster than Abbott, whose MitraClip volumes grew just 6% versus our 14% on the AetherClip device. Emerging markets like LATAM and India added 30 bps combined, driven by our low-cost BioAdapt coatings reducing infection rates by 37% in high-volume public hospitals.

Strategically, we're not resting on these gains. We've doubled down on R&D, investing $420 million this year—8% of revenue—into our PrecisionFlow platform, integrating generative AI for predictive hemodynamics that could boost procedure efficiency by 20%. M&A remains key: our $1.2 billion acquisition of NeuroVasc Therapeutics last quarter added 400 bps in neuromodulation share, positioning us against Medtronic's Symplicity Spyral. Pricing discipline is critical too—we held ASPs flat at $26,200 for TAVR while competitors conceded 3-5%, preserving 62% gross margins. And on supply chain resilience, our U.S. and Ireland fabs now cover 85% of North American demand, mitigating the chip shortages that plagued Stryker's orthopedics peers.

Looking forward, we see sustained tailwinds from aging demographics—U.S. TAVR-eligible patients up 12% to 1.2 million—and regulatory momentum, with EU MDR compliance behind us. Risks include potential U.S. election-year changes to Medicare Part B device pass-throughs and intensifying China localization mandates, but our 45% localization rate there gives us an edge. Overall, we're confident in delivering another 150-200 bps of share gain in FY24, targeting 26-27% in core segments.

Moving on to capital equipment vs consumables mix trends.

Before diving deeper, I'd like to highlight a key metric that underscores the resiliency and growth profile of our business: the capital equipment versus consumables revenue mix. In the medtech industry, capital equipment—think our flagship imaging systems, neurostimulation platforms, and next-gen orthopedic navigation robots—represents the high-margin, lumpy upfront sales that build our installed base. Consumables, on the other hand, include our high-volume, annuity-like streams from single-use catheters, disposable endoscopic guides, neuromodulation leads, and our growing portfolio of bioabsorbable implants and drug-eluting stents. This mix is a critical leading indicator of long-term revenue predictability, pull-through dynamics, and overall profitability.

In Q2, our overall revenue mix shifted to 32% capital equipment and 68% consumables, up from 38%/62% in the prior-year quarter and meaningfully ahead of our five-year average of 42%/58%. On a dollar basis, capital equipment came in at $285 million, flat year-over-year as we lap a strong Q2 '23 comp driven by a U.S. hospital capex surge post-COVID backlog. Consumables, however, accelerated to $595 million, delivering 22% reported growth—or 19% organic—fueled by procedural volume tailwinds and share gains.

Zooming out to the trailing 12 months, consumables now represent 67% of total revenue, a 450-basis-point improvement YoY, while capital has held steady at around $1.1 billion annually. This trend mirrors what we're seeing across peers like Intuitive Surgical, where da Vinci consumables have pushed their mix beyond 75%, or Boston Scientific's Watchman franchise, which is driving electrophysiology consumables to over 70% in their CRM segment. Our consumables growth outpaced the broader market—per our internal tracking against IQVIA procedure data, U.S. structural heart procedures grew 14% YoY, but our relevant consumables grew 25% thanks to deeper penetration.

Several dynamics are at play here. First, hospital capex cycles remain constrained globally. U.S. hospitals, facing margin pressures from labor shortages and rising supply costs, deferred 15-20% of planned capital buys in Q2, per HIMSS data—similar to what Stryker reported in their ortho robotics installed base updates. This has pushed customers toward our capex-light bundles, like our modular imaging suites, which emphasize software upgrades and service contracts over full-system replacements.

Second, procedural volumes are booming, particularly in high-acuity areas. Our neurovascular consumables, including aspiration catheters akin to Penumbra's Lightning system, saw 28% growth on the back of stroke intervention volumes up 18% YoY. In orthopedics, our single-use navigation trackers and cement mixing systems benefited from outpatient shift—ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) now account for 22% of our U.S. ortho consumables, up from 15% two years ago.

Third, pricing and utilization are holding firm. Average selling prices (ASPs) for consumables were up 3% YoY, supported by our premium positioning in drug-coated balloons and bioresorbable scaffolds. Installed base utilization rates improved to 82% globally—up 300 basis points—driven by our AI-enhanced procedure optimization software, which boosts case efficiency by 12-15% per our clinical studies.

We've been aggressive on innovation to widen the moat. Our Q2 launch of the NeuroPulse 2.0 neuromodulation platform—a capital system with proprietary rechargeable leads—has already secured 150 U.S. placements, with expected 4x pull-through on disposables over the first year, mirroring Medtronic's Percept RC trajectory. In endoscopy, our single-use DuoScope tips, compatible with legacy capital scopes, captured 12% market share in GI procedures within three months, cannibalizing reusables and driving a 35% consumables ramp in that sub-segment.

Looking ahead, we're investing $250 million in R&D for our next-gen robotics initiative—third-gen arms with fully disposable end-effectors—to address sterilization bottlenecks. Early pilots show 25% higher procedure throughput, which should lift consumables attachment rates from 65% to 75% by FY25.

Regionally, the mix varies significantly, reflecting reimbursement and infrastructure dynamics. In the U.S. (52% of revenue), consumables at 72% mix, up 400 bps YoY, propelled by ASC proliferation—over 6,500 centers now, per ASCA—and Medicare Advantage tailwinds favoring high-volume, low-capex sites. Capital softened to 28% amid capex scrutiny, but our hospital pipeline remains robust at $2.5 billion.

EMEA (28% of revenue): More balanced at 58% consumables, with capital at 42%. Growth here was muted at 12% for consumables due to DRG reimbursement cuts in Germany and Italy, but our Value Analysis Committee wins in the UK NHS for our embolic protection devices offset this, gaining 8 points of share.

APAC (15% of revenue): Fastest consumables growth at 32% YoY, pushing mix to 65%. China procedure volumes surged 25% post-NMPA approvals for our structural heart consumables, while Japan's aging demographics boosted neurostim leads. Capital here is cyclical, down 5% on hospital consolidation, but our partnerships with local players like Terumo are building a 500-unit installed base for pull-through.

Rest of World (5%): Emerging markets like Brazil and India saw consumables double-digit growth on affordable single-use portfolios.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on evolving into a razor-and-blade powerhouse. Our goal is 70%+ consumables mix by 2026, which at current growth rates implies $3.5 billion in recurring revenue—high-margin, with gross margins expanding 200 bps to 72% this year. To get there, we're prioritizing installed base expansion targeting 10% annual growth to 45,000 units via trade-in programs and emerging market greenfield builds; pull-through optimization with AI analytics dashboards for customers to maximize utilization; M&A pipeline with $1 billion dry powder for bolt-on consumables plays; and risk mitigation by diversifying beyond pure-play capital, with 40% of consumables now procedure-agnostic.

This consumables-led mix shift not only de-risks our model—lowering revenue volatility by 25% over five years—but positions us for mid-teens organic growth through the decade.

Next, revenue and margin guidance for the next quarter/year.

I'll now turn to our outlook for the third quarter of 2024 and our full-year fiscal 2025 guidance. Our guidance reflects a continued robust demand environment across our core franchises—Cardiovascular, Orthopedics, and Neuromodulation—driven by favorable demographics, procedural growth, and our leadership in minimally invasive technologies. We've baked in some conservatism around potential supply chain headwinds from ongoing Red Sea disruptions and U.S. reimbursement dynamics under the CY2025 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, but we're well-positioned with our diversified manufacturing footprint and pricing discipline.

Q3 revenue guidance: $2.45 billion to $2.50 billion. This implies year-over-year growth of 9% to 11%, or 10% to 12% on an organic, constant-currency basis, excluding the impact of our recent acquisition of NeuroPulse Therapeutics, which closed in Q2 and is already delivering $50 million in annualized run-rate revenue from their next-gen spinal cord stimulator platform.

Core revenue trends remain strong: Cardiovascular segment (55% of revenue): Expect 12-14% organic growth, fueled by our Watchman FLX Pro LAA closure device, which saw 25% procedural adoption growth in Q2, and the U.S. launch of our EluNIR R drug-eluting stent, capturing share from Boston Scientific's Synergy platform amid competitive pricing. Structural heart procedures are tracking above our initial 15% market growth forecast. Orthopedics (25% of revenue): Mid-single-digit growth, with our Mako robotic-arm system hitting 1,200 installed bases globally—up 18% YoY—driving recurring implant revenue. Hip and knee revision rates remain elevated post-COVID, supporting our Triathlon Total Knee System. Neuromodulation and Other (20% of revenue): 8-10% growth, led by our ReviX HF deep brain stimulation system for Parkinson's, with FDA approval for expanded DBS indications expected in Q1.

Regionally: U.S. (65% of revenue): 11-13% growth, bolstered by our direct sales force expansion to 4,500 reps and favorable site-of-care shifts to ASCs, where our portfolio penetration is now 35%. EUMEA (20%): 6-8% organic growth at constant currency, navigating HTA delays in Germany and France but offset by strong U.K. NICE reimbursement for our Evoque TMVR valve, rivaling Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien. APAC & Rest of World (15%): Double-digit growth, with China ramping to 20% of segment revenue via our J-V partnership with Mindray for localized Ortho robotics production, mitigating tariff risks.

Q3 Adjusted Gross Margin: 68.5% to 69.5%, up 150 basis points sequentially from Q2's reported level, driven by manufacturing mix shift toward higher-margin disposables (now 62% of revenue), $75 million in productivity gains from our SmartFactory 2.0 initiative in Galway, Ireland, leveraging AI-optimized CNC machining for stents and leads—reducing COGS by 12%, and favorable forex with the euro at 1.08 USD providing a 50 bps tailwind.

Q3 Adjusted Operating Margin: 24.5% to 25.5%, reflecting disciplined OpEx at 44% of revenue, including $120 million in R&D investment (up 5% QoQ) for our pipeline, headlined by the Polaris robotic navigation platform for EP ablations, set for CE Mark in H1'25.

Full-Year FY25 Revenue Guidance: $10.0 billion to $10.3 billion. This represents 7% to 10% total growth, or 8% to 11% organic constant-currency growth—above our long-term 7-9% target. We'd exit FY25 above $10.5 billion in run-rate revenue, positioning us for sustained double-digit compounding. Key drivers: Procedural tailwinds with global medtech procedure volumes growing 5-7%, per Leerink Partners data, with our exposure to high-growth areas like TAVR at 20% market growth and SGLT2-driven HFpEF devices; new product ramps contributing $1.2 billion from launches, including the full U.S. rollout of our Sentinel Cerebral Protection System (now standard-of-care in 40% of TAVR cases) and APAC expansion of the Hugo RAS robotic surgery system, challenging Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci dominance at a 30% lower ASP; M&A accretion expecting another bolt-on deal in electrophysiology, targeting 10% ROIC.

FY25 Adjusted Gross Margin: 69.0% to 70.0%, expansion of 100-150 bps YoY, propelled by scale efficiencies from our $500 million Galway expansion, targeting 75% U.S. localization to de-risk tariffs; pricing actions netting +1.5% (ASP uplift on premium robotics and CV disposables), countering 2-3% medical inflation; supply chain resilience with dual-sourcing titanium and nitinol from U.S./Vietnam facilities, insulating against rare earth volatility.

FY25 Adjusted Operating Margin: 25.5% to 26.5%, with OpEx at 43-44% of revenue, including R&D at 12.5% (up from 12% in FY24) to fuel 15+ IDE submissions. Adjusted EPS guidance of $5.80 to $6.00, implying 10-14% growth, assumes a 25% effective tax rate, 100 million diluted shares (post $1.5 billion buyback authorization), and capex at 4.5% of revenue.

Free cash flow outlook remains strong at $2.0-2.2 billion (20-22% FCF margin), supporting 40% payout via dividends and buybacks. We're confident in delivering on these targets, underpinned by our 65% U.S. market share leadership in key segments and innovation moat—evidenced by 28% of current revenue from products less than 5 years old.

Then, key assumptions underlying the guidance.

Now, turning to the key assumptions underpinning our full-year 2024 guidance, we're projecting consolidated revenue growth of 8% to 10% at constant currency, or $4.65 billion to $4.72 billion, with adjusted diluted EPS of $4.50 to $4.70. This represents a solid acceleration from our 6% organic growth in 2023, driven by our structural tailwinds in high-growth segments like structural heart, neuromodulation, and robotics-assisted surgery.

Let me walk you through these, grounded in our detailed bottom-up planning process, incorporating real-time procedure data from our CRM systems, hospital surveys, and macroeconomic modeling. We've stress-tested against downside scenarios, including a 10% pullback in elective procedure volumes or a 2% FX headwind.

First, procedure volumes and market dynamics, the primary driver contributing about 60% of growth. Our guidance embeds mid-single-digit growth in global procedure volumes, aligning with IQVIA and GlobalData forecasts of 4-6% expansion in the med device market. This is fueled by aging demographics—global over-65 population up 3% YoY—and a shift toward minimally invasive procedures, where we hold leading positions.

U.S. (65% of Revenue): We assume 5-7% procedure growth, reflecting sustained OR utilization at 85-90% (up from 75% in 2022 post-COVID backlog). Elective orthopedics and structural heart volumes—like TAVR and MitraClip analogs—should grow 8-10%, supported by CMS reimbursement stability under the 2024 OPPS final rule, which preserved pass-through status for our next-gen Perimeter transcatheter valve. We're also baking in share gains of 100-150 bps in robotics, where our Endeavor system captured 12% U.S. market share in Q2 via 25 new system placements.

Europe (20% of Revenue): More muted 3-5% volume growth due to reimbursement headwinds from DRG bundling in Germany and Italy's tariff cuts. However, our CE Mark for the NeuroStim DBS platform positions us for 15% growth in neuromodulation, outpacing Medtronic's trajectory amid their recent supply constraints.

Asia-Pacific and Emerging Markets (15% of Revenue): High-teens growth at 15-18%, led by China (post-NMPA approval for our VisionAI retinal scanner) and India (elective spine procedures up 20% YoY). We're assuming normalized supply from our Suzhou facility, avoiding last year's 5% shipment delays from resin shortages.

Second, pricing and mix shift, contributing about 2 points to growth. ASP inflation of 1-2%, flat to slightly positive after payer pushback. We're modeling a favorable mix shift: high-acuity products like our RhythmSync CRM devices (25% gross margins premium over legacy pacemakers) and Endura robotic consumables growing to 35% of revenue mix from 30%. This offsets ~1% erosion from GPO contracts with Vizient and Premier. Competitive dynamics remain constructive—no major entrants in our coronary stents franchise, where we trail Boston Scientific's Synergy but lead on deliverability metrics.

Third, supply chain and cost assumptions. Core gross margin expansion to 62-64% (up 100 bps YoY), assuming raw material costs (PTFE, nitinol) stabilize at +3% inflation, down from 8% in 2023. Semiconductor lead times for our AI-enabled imaging chips have normalized to 12 weeks from 26, thanks to dual-sourcing with TSMC and U.S. partners. Freight costs flat as Red Sea disruptions ease. OpEx as a percentage of revenue at 32-33%, with R&D at 12% ($560 million), funding 15 Phase III trials including our pulsed-field ablation catheter for AFib—a $5B TAM opportunity rivaling Johnson & Johnson's Varipulse.

Fourth, strategic initiatives and innovation pipeline. Guidance assumes on-track execution of our MedTech 2.0 strategy: FDA Approvals with PMA for two structural heart devices (Q2/Q4 2024), unlocking $300M incremental revenue; Digital Health with 20% growth in connected care, our HealthLink platform integrating wearables data into EHRs, targeting 500K patients like Abbott's Libre but for neuromodulation; M&A Synergies with full-year $50M savings from our $1.2B acquisition of NeuroVive, bolstering 15% CAGR in brain-computer interfaces; Sustainability with 10% reduction in Scope 3 emissions supports EU MDR compliance, avoiding fines seen by peers like LivaNova.

Fifth, macro and FX sensitivities. A stronger USD (EUR at 1.08, CNY at 7.2) creates a 1-2% headwind; we're hedged 70% for FY24. Hospital capex flat amid 5% Fed funds rate, but leasing penetration (40% of robotics installs) mitigates this. Inflation at 3% flows through to wages but is offset by productivity gains from our LEAN Sigma initiatives (15% throughput improvement in sterile packaging).

In summary, this guidance reflects our resilient franchise, with 70% of growth from secular drivers like TAVR volumes (projected 15% TAM CAGR to 2030) and AI diagnostics. Risks include prolonged hospital staffing shortages (OR nurse vacancy at 18%) or China stimulus delays, but our 45% U.S. market share in key segments and $2.5B cash position provide ample buffer.

Finally, gross margin trends and supply chain commentary.

Before I wrap up, let's dive deeper into our gross margin trends and supply chain dynamics, which continue to be a cornerstone of our operational resilience in the Medical Devices sector.

We delivered a Q2 GAAP gross margin of 67.8%, up 210 basis points year-over-year from 65.7% in Q2 2023, and 40 basis points sequentially from Q1 2024's 67.4%. On an adjusted non-GAAP basis, excluding certain one-time charges related to our legacy ERP migration, we hit 68.2%—our strongest quarterly performance since pre-pandemic levels. For the first half of 2024, adjusted gross margins stand at 67.9%, positioning us at the high end of our peer group, comparable to Abbott's Nutrition and Diagnostics segment or Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci platform margins in the mid-to-high 60s.

This expansion was driven by three key levers, all aligned with our Margin+3 initiative: Favorable product mix shift (120 bps contribution), with structural shift toward higher-margin consumables and services. Structural heart disposables—our next-gen TAVR valves and transcatheter mitral repair kits—grew 28% YoY to represent 42% of total revenue, up from 37% last year. These carry gross margins north of 75%, materially outpacing our capital equipment like the AetherFlex robotic-assisted surgery systems, which grew 15% YoY but have margins in the low 50s due to ASP erosion from competitive bundling. Orthopedics also contributed, with our 3D-printed titanium implants for spinal fusion boosting mix by 5 points as elective procedures rebounded.

Manufacturing efficiencies and pricing discipline (60 bps contribution): We've realized $45 million in annualized savings from our automation roadmap, including Industry 4.0 cobots at our Galway facility, reducing labor content in neurostimulation device assembly by 18%. Yield rates on our semiconductor-integrated CGM sensors improved to 98.2% from 95.4% YoY, thanks to our partnership with TSMC for custom ASICs. On pricing, U.S. net pricing held flat at -1.2% sequentially, cushioned by Value-Based Care contracts with payers like UnitedHealth's Optum, which now cover 22% of our U.S. cardiac rhythm management volume. In Europe, ex-VAT pricing grew 2.1% amid favorable reimbursement under the new In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR).

Supply chain tailwinds (30 bps contribution): Forex tailwinds from a weaker euro and yen added 15 bps, while lower freight rates post-Red Sea peak shaved another 15 bps off COGS.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 adjusted gross margins of 68.0% to 68.5%, with full-year guidance narrowed to 67.5%-68.0%, implying 150-200 bps of YoY expansion. Risks remain around potential CMS cuts to the IPPS for FY2025, but we're mitigating via our 40/60 hardware-to-consumables ASP ladder.

Shifting to supply chain—an area where we've transformed vulnerability into competitive advantage. The MedTech sector faced brutal headwinds in 2022-2023: semiconductor shortages delayed Abbott's FreeStyle Libre production, nitinol wire constraints hit Boston Scientific's Watchman LAAO devices, and resin inflation squeezed margins across orthopedics. We've de-risked aggressively under our Supply Chain Fortress program: Single-source dependency now below 5% for critical components, down from 22% in 2021. We've shifted 35% of electronics assembly to our Tijuana, Mexico facility, reducing APAC exposure from 55% to 38%.
